definition.text: Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment.

facts.text: Waste can be hazardous because it is toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable.
As of 2022, humanity produced 300–500 million metric tons of hazardous waste a year.
Common sources include solvents, batteries and by-products of metal refining.
Many ordinary businesses, such as dry cleaners, car repair shops, hospitals and photo labs, generate it.
Mismanaged hazardous waste can pollute the air, raising illness and death, and contaminate groundwater and soil.
It is regulated at local, national and international levels.

definition.text: Hazardous waste is disposed of by treating and stabilising it for secure landfills, burning it, or recycling it.

facts.text: Incinerators burn it at 870–1400 °C, greatly shrinking it, but the leftover ash and gases can also be hazardous.
Some hazardous materials, such as lead–acid batteries and circuit boards, can be recycled into new products.
Landfills for such waste need barriers along their foundations to stop groundwater contamination.
Plasma treatment above 3000 °C turns waste into inert rock-like slag; it is very expensive but suits persistent pollutants such as PCBs.

definition.text: Poorer people and social minorities face a higher risk of exposure to hazardous waste and its pollution.

facts.text: An Austrian study found people living near industrial sites are more often unemployed, less educated and twice as likely to be immigrants.
Groups who rely on local land and streams for food and water, including Native Americans, face multiplied risk.

definition.text: Hazardous waste has been shipped from rich countries to poorer ones with weaker rules, prompting the Basel Convention to curb the trade.

facts.text: As laws such as RCRA raised disposal costs in developed nations in the 1970s, the waste trade to poorer countries grew fast.
In 1990 OECD countries exported around 1.8 million tons of hazardous waste.
199 countries signed the 1992 Basel Convention to stop this flow.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 includes sound management of chemicals and wastes throughout their life cycle.

definition.text: A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish.

facts.text: It is the oldest and most common way of disposing of waste, though systematic burial with daily and final covers only began in the 1940s.
The modern sanitary landfill is an engineered facility that separates and confines waste, widely adopted in the 1960s and 1970s to end open dumps.
Landfills take up much land and pose environmental risks such as groundwater and soil contamination.
Nuisances include dust, odour, noise, disease-carrying rats and flies, and lower local property values.
Permitting a US landfill generally takes five to seven years and costs millions of dollars.
Closed landfills are often reused as parks, bike courses or solar farms.

definition.text: A sanitary landfill works as a biological reactor in which microbes break organic waste down into simpler, less toxic compounds over several phases.

facts.text: First, oxygen trapped in the waste supports aerobic breakdown until microbes use it up.
In the acid phase, fatty acids build up and leachate pH falls from about 7.5 to 5.6.
In the longest phase, methane-making microbes turn the acids into methane and CO2.
Finally methane production almost stops as nutrients run short and oxygen seeps back in.

definition.text: Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water seeps through landfill waste, picking up organic matter, heavy metals and other pollutants.

facts.text: If not contained, it can contaminate groundwater.
Modern landfills use impermeable liners several metres thick, stable sites and collection systems to capture it.
Full landfills are sealed to stop rain entering and forming new leachate.

definition.text: Landfill gas is the mix of mainly methane and carbon dioxide produced when microbes digest organic waste without oxygen.

facts.text: On average it is about half methane and slightly less than half CO2.
Landfills are the 3rd largest emitter of methane worldwide.
Well-managed landfills collect the gas, either flaring it or using it to generate electricity; more than 850 US landfills recover it.
Capturing landfill methane is a common type of carbon offset project.

definition.text: Aftercare is the long period after a landfill is full and capped, when liners, gas capture and leachate treatment continue to limit harm.

facts.text: Aftercare may last from several decades up to forever, costing more than 20 million euros per landfill in the Netherlands.
Because sealed waste keeps its power to pollute, replacing liners and treating leachate is an indefinite requirement.

definition.text: Alternatives to landfill include waste reduction and recycling, waste-to-energy incineration, anaerobic digestion, composting and other treatments.

facts.text: Depending on local economics and incentives, these can be made cheaper than landfilling.
Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland have banned landfilling untreated waste.
The UK taxes biodegradable waste sent to landfill, and England set up a scheme for councils to trade landfill quotas.
The zero waste concept aims to minimise landfill volume.
